---
title: Connect a web page
description: Let a page in a browser register itself with an instance, get the owner's approval in a small window, and read the owner's data with the token it receives.
---

A web page connects the way any [app signs in with OAuth](/build/authenticate), with every step taken by the page's own script. The instance needs **no setup** and the page needs **no key**. The page registers itself, the owner approves it once, and the instance then lets the page's address call it from a browser.

The steps follow the [authorization code grant](/build/authenticate#connect-an-app-with-oauth) and cover what a browser changes about it.

## What the page needs

- **An `https` address.** A web page registers as a web client, whose redirect addresses must be `https` and off the loopback. A page served from `http://localhost` can't connect this way; serve it from an `https` address with a real host name.
- **A callback page** at the redirect address, for the approval window to hand the code back. The callback step below shows it.
- **An instance the browser can reach.** When a page on a public address calls an instance on a private-network or loopback address, Chrome asks the person for Local Network Access permission before the page's first request, and blocks the request if they decline.

## Connect the page

<Steps>
<Step>

### Find the endpoints

The discovery documents answer a request from any origin, with no credential, so a page that isn't yet approved can read them. The one to read names the registration, authorization and token endpoints:

```ts title="connect.ts"
const instance = "https://marfa.example.com";

const meta = await (
  await fetch(`${instance}/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/auth`)
).json();
// meta.registration_endpoint, meta.authorization_endpoint, meta.token_endpoint
```

</Step>
<Step>

### Register the page

Registration takes no credential and answers any origin, so the page registers itself from the browser. Name the page's callback address, which sets the origin the owner approves:

```ts title="connect.ts"
const redirectUri = `${location.origin}/callback`;

const registered = await (
  await fetch(meta.registration_endpoint, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      client_name: "Reading page",
      redirect_uris: [redirectUri],
      token_endpoint_auth_method: "none",
      grant_types: ["authorization_code"],
      response_types: ["code"],
      scope: "core.note:read core.note:write",
    }),
  })
).json();
const clientId: string = registered.client_id;
```

Marfa answers `201` with the `client_id`. A page keeps no secret, so `"token_endpoint_auth_method": "none"` registers a public client that proves itself with PKCE.

A registration takes at most 32 KiB and 10 redirect addresses. A larger body is refused `413 request_too_large`, and more addresses `400 invalid_redirect_uri`. A registration nobody approves is removed after a day idle, as [Housekeeping](/run/housekeeping) describes, so register again at each connection until the owner approves, then keep the `client_id`.

</Step>
<Step>

### Make the PKCE pair and a state

Marfa accepts only PKCE with `S256`. Make a random verifier, its challenge, and a `state` of your own:

```ts title="connect.ts"
const base64url = (bytes: ArrayBuffer | Uint8Array) =>
  btoa(String.fromCharCode(...new Uint8Array(bytes)))
    .replace(/\+/g, "-")
    .replace(/\//g, "_")
    .replace(/=+$/, "");

const random = (size: number) => base64url(crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(size)));
const verifier = random(32);
const state = random(16);
const challenge = base64url(
  await crypto.subtle.digest("SHA-256", new TextEncoder().encode(verifier)),
);
```

</Step>
<Step>

### Open the approval window

Listen for the answer first, because it can come back before the next line returns. Every tab of the page hears every callback, so keep only the answer that carries this connection's `state`. Then open the authorization endpoint in a small window, from a click, because browsers block a window that no click opened:

```ts title="connect.ts"
const answered = new Promise<URLSearchParams>((resolve) => {
  const channel = new BroadcastChannel("marfa-approval");
  channel.onmessage = (event) => {
    const answer = new URLSearchParams(event.data);
    if (answer.get("state") !== state) return;
    channel.close();
    resolve(answer);
  };
});

const authorize = new URL(meta.authorization_endpoint);
authorize.search = new URLSearchParams({
  response_type: "code",
  client_id: clientId,
  redirect_uri: redirectUri,
  scope: "core.note:read core.note:write",
  state,
  code_challenge: challenge,
  code_challenge_method: "S256",
}).toString();
open(authorize, "marfa-approval", "popup,width=480,height=640");
```

The window asks the owner to sign in if needed. It then shows the page's name, a caution that Marfa has not verified it, **the page's origin**, and a choice between **Full access**, which grants everything the page asks for, and **Choose access**, which lets the owner give less. [Approve an app](/run/manage-apps#approve-an-app) describes the choices and when approval needs a recent sign-in.

</Step>
<Step>

### Hand the code back from the callback page

When the owner decides, Marfa sends the window to the callback address with `code`, `state` and `iss`, or with `error=access_denied` if the owner declined.

Marfa's sign-in and approval pages send `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin`, so the browser cuts the window off from the page that opened it. The page can't read `window.opener` or the window's address. The callback page runs at the page's own origin, so it passes the result over a `BroadcastChannel`, which only that origin can hear:

```html title="callback.html"
<!doctype html>
<title>Connecting</title>
<script>
  new BroadcastChannel("marfa-approval").postMessage(location.search);
  close();
</script>
```

The main page waits on the channel it opened before the window, and checks the answer:

```ts title="connect.ts"
const answer = await answered;

if (answer.get("error")) throw new Error(`not approved: ${answer.get("error")}`);
const code = answer.get("code")!;
```

An owner who closes the window sends nothing, so give the page a way to cancel the wait.

</Step>
<Step>

### Exchange the code

Send the code and the verifier to the token endpoint, as a form. A public client sends no secret:

```ts title="connect.ts"
const token = await (
  await fetch(meta.token_endpoint, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" },
    body: new URLSearchParams({
      grant_type: "authorization_code",
      code,
      redirect_uri: redirectUri,
      client_id: clientId,
      code_verifier: verifier,
    }),
  })
).json();
```

```json title="Response" status="200"
{
  "access_token": "marfa_at_…",
  "expires_in": 3600,
  "expires_at": 1791593756,
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "scope": "core.note:read"
}
```

A code works once. `scope` lists what the owner chose, which can be less than the page asked for.

</Step>
<Step>

### Make a data request

Send the access token in the `Authorization` header, as for any key:

```ts title="connect.ts"
const response = await fetch(`${instance}/items?type=core.note&limit=5`, {
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token.access_token}` },
});
const notes = await response.json();
```

```http title="Request"
GET /items?type=core.note&limit=5
Authorization: Bearer marfa_at_…
```

Don't send `credentials: "include"`: Marfa never allows credentials on a cross-origin answer, so the page works only with the token it holds. [List items](/api-reference/items/listItems) has every parameter.

The token expires after `expires_in` seconds. To get another, open the approval window again and exchange the new code: an owner who is signed in and approved these scopes already goes straight back with a code. To end the approval, [revoke access](/build/authenticate#revoke-access).

</Step>
</Steps>

## Redirect the whole page instead

For a browser that blocks windows, or a page that can lose its place and recover it, skip the window and send the browser itself to the authorization address. The page leaves and comes back, so the opener policy never matters, and the callback page is the page itself.

Before leaving, keep the `verifier`, `state` and `client_id` in `sessionStorage`. On return, read `code` and `state` from the query string, check `state`, then exchange the code.

## What the approval allows

Approving the page lets the origin (scheme, host and port) of each `https` redirect address it registered call the instance from a browser, until the last connected app on that origin is disconnected. Before approval, only discovery and registration answer the page.

**The access token is the only authority.** The origin lets the browser deliver answers to the page and gives it nothing else. A form posted from that origin to the sign-in or approval address is refused `403 forbidden`, so the page never acts as the owner.

An operator who trusts an origin in advance names it in `CORS_ORIGINS`, as [Settings](/run/settings#every-environment-setting) shows. A native app's redirect address, where a program on a device listens, allows no origin.

## If a step fails

| What the page sees | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Registration answers `413 request_too_large` or `400 invalid_redirect_uri` | The body is over 32 KiB, or an address isn't `https`, is on the loopback, doesn't parse, or the registration names more than 10. |
| The code never reaches the page | The callback page is missing, or the page reads `window.opener`, which the opener policy cuts. |
| A request is blocked with no response | The owner hasn't approved the page, declined it or disconnected it, or the page's origin isn't the origin of any redirect address it registered. |
| The token endpoint answers `400 invalid_grant` | The code was used already, or the verifier doesn't match its challenge. |

The rules behind this guide are in the [keys and sign-in](https://github.com/withmarfa/marfa/blob/main/conformance/spec/keys-and-oauth.md#web-pages) chapter of the contract, which names each of the limits above.
